Summary: The evidence indicates a topical / lexical bias in model B (B − A) rather than a clear change in decoding strategy or sentiment. Concretely, B’s residuals push logits toward tokens about (1) professional/academic credentials and status (dissertation, doctoral, professional/professionalism, undergraduate, honors, technical/engineering, etc.) and (2) culinary/restaurant/cooking vocabulary (Cook, cooking, Cooking, culinary, restaurant, baking, oven, Cake, microwave, hot, etc.). The effect is strongest on the early token positions (especially position 1) and in the later middle-to-final layers (layers ~16–25), per the L2 norms.

Why I conclude this
- Logit-lens top tokens: across many high-norm (layer,position) cells the top target tokens are repeatedly words like "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional"/"professionalism", "Professional", and similarly repeated culinary tokens ("Cook", "cooking", "culinary", "restaurant", "baking", "oven", "Cake", "hot"). That pattern is systematic across many cells and layers.
- Norms: the difference magnitude is concentrated in later layers (especially layers 21–25) and is very large at position 1 (p1) across layers, indicating the change will affect what the model tends to generate right after the first token and that it is a high-level / semantic effect.
- No single narrow objective is uniquely supported: the tokens point to a combination of professional/academic and culinary domains (and a few scattered tokens like "billionaire", "Obama", "Innovation"), so the safest interpretation is a topical/lexical bias (more probability mass on words about credentials/professions and cooking/restaurant matters) rather than a specific named capability.

If you want, I can:
- Run patchscope-style continuations or provide more focused logit-lens outputs (e.g., full probability shifts for a few prompts) to test whether B actually produces more recipe/restaurant or résumé-style text in practice.
